stories.title: Tajinderpal Singh Toor qualifies for the Commonwealth Games shot put final, setting up a duel with defending champion Tom Walsh
key_points: India's shot put national record holder **Tajinderpal Singh Toor** threw **20.14m** to qualify for Thursday's final.
New Zealand's **Tom Walsh**, the defending Commonwealth Games champion, topped qualifying with a first-round **21.03m**.
Fellow Indian **Samardeep Singh Gill** also advanced to the final.
Toor is chasing his **first-ever Commonwealth Games medal** in the event.
The final takes place **Friday, July 31**.
stories.background: **Tajinderpal Singh Toor** holds the Indian national record in shot put and has been one of India's most consistent throwers for years, but a Commonwealth Games medal in the event has eluded him so far. **Tom Walsh** of New Zealand is the reigning Commonwealth Games champion and one of the most dominant shot putters in the world, making him the clear favorite heading into Friday's final.
stories.what_happened: In Wednesday's qualifying round at the **2026 Commonwealth Games** in Glasgow, Toor sealed his spot in the final with a **20.14m** throw on his second attempt, finishing second overall behind Walsh's opening throw of **21.03m**. Fellow Indian competitor Samardeep Singh Gill also progressed through qualifying. Both will now compete in Friday's medal final against Walsh and the rest of the qualified field.
stories.why_it_matters: A shot put medal would be a breakthrough for Toor, who has long been talked about as one of India's best field-event prospects without a Commonwealth Games podium finish to show for it.
stories.ripple_effects: A strong Indian showing in the shot put final adds to the country's field-event medal push in Glasgow, alongside javelin and long jump, and raises Toor's profile heading into future global meets.
stories.why_now: Qualifying concluded Wednesday, setting the field for Friday's final at the ongoing Commonwealth Games.
stories.watch_next: The men's shot put final on Friday, July 31, where Toor faces defending champion Tom Walsh.
stories.the_lesson: In throwing events, qualifying position doesn't decide medals — Toor goes into the final needing to beat, not just match, the best throw of the day to have a real shot at gold.

stories.title: Neeraj Chopra opens his Commonwealth Games javelin title defense in Glasgow qualifying
key_points: Chopra begins his bid to **reclaim the men's javelin title** he won at **Gold Coast 2018**, in today's qualifying round in Glasgow.
He **missed Birmingham 2022** with injury, making this his first CWG javelin appearance in **eight years**.
He arrives in form, having thrown **85.69m for fourth place** at the Doha Diamond League, well clear of the qualifying mark.
Fellow Indians **Yash Vir Singh and Rohit Yadav** also compete in the qualifying round alongside him.
The **final is in the early hours of August 1 (IST)** — a two-day wait after today's qualifying.
stories.background: **Neeraj Chopra** is India's most decorated track and field athlete, best known for winning India's first-ever Olympic gold in athletics at Tokyo 2020. He won Commonwealth Games javelin gold at **Gold Coast in 2018**, but a groin injury forced him out of the **2022 Birmingham Games** entirely, leaving him without a CWG title defense until now. Since then he has remained one of the world's most consistent javelin throwers, competing for global and Olympic medals against rivals including Pakistan's Arshad Nadeem.
stories.what_happened: The men's javelin throw qualifying round is being held today in Glasgow, part of the athletics program at the **2026 Commonwealth Games**. Chopra needs to hit an automatic qualifying distance or finish among the top throwers to advance to Friday's medal round. He goes in with strong recent form, having thrown **85.69m** for fourth place at the Doha Diamond League — a distance well above what's typically needed to advance. India has entered three men in the event: Chopra, Yash Vir Singh, and Rohit Yadav. The final will take place in the early hours of **August 1 (IST)**.
stories.why_it_matters: Javelin is one of India's most reliable Commonwealth Games medal hopes, and Chopra is the country's biggest global sporting star — his results move national attention and sponsorship interest well beyond athletics fans.
stories.ripple_effects: A strong qualifying showing builds expectation for gold on Friday and adds to India's medal tally push in Glasgow; an upset or injury scare would be a major story in Indian sport regardless of the outcome.
stories.why_now: The Commonwealth Games 2026 athletics program in Glasgow scheduled javelin qualifying for today, with the final two days later.
stories.watch_next: The men's javelin final, in the early hours of August 1 IST.

key_terms.definition: In athletics, a preliminary stage where throwers or jumpers must hit a set distance or finish in the top group to advance to the medal final.

stories.the_lesson: Even the best athletes can lose years of competition to injury — Chopra's eight-year gap between CWG javelin appearances shows how fragile even elite athletic careers are to a single setback.

stories.title: Dilip Gavit becomes India's first male para-athletics gold medallist at the Commonwealth Games
key_points: **Dilip Mahadu Gavit** won gold in the men's **T47 100m** with a **Games record of 10.71 seconds**.
He is the **first Indian male athlete to win a Commonwealth Games gold in para athletics**.
India took a **historic 1-2 finish** — teammate **Mohammed Basil Morssinganakth** took silver in the same race.
It was India's **third gold and 15th medal overall** at the Glasgow Games.
Gavit, 23, from **Nashik**, dedicated the win to coach Vaijanath Kale, who spotted him working on his family farm.
stories.background: The **T47 classification** covers athletes with an impairment in one arm, and the Commonwealth Games — a multi-sport event held every four years among Commonwealth nations — has increasingly integrated para-sport medals directly into the main competition and medal table. Indian para-athletics has produced strong performers at the Paralympics, but a Commonwealth Games gold from a male para-athlete had eluded the country until now. Gavit's coach, **Vaijanath Kale**, discovered him while he was working on his family's farm in Nashik, Maharashtra, and helped transform him into a competitive sprinter.
stories.what_happened: On **July 29 (Day 6)** of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, **Dilip Mahadu Gavit** won the men's **T47 100m** final in **10.71 seconds**, setting a new Games record and becoming the **first Indian male athlete to win a Commonwealth Games gold medal in para athletics**. His teammate **Mohammed Basil Morssinganakth** finished right behind him for silver, giving India a **historic 1-2 finish** in the event. The gold was India's **third of the Games** and its **15th medal overall**, moving the country to 8th on the medal table. Gavit, 23, dedicated the win — on the Hindu festival of Guru Purnima, which honors teachers — to his coach Vaijanath Kale, who discovered his talent while Gavit was working on his family's farm and helped guide his career since.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a genuine milestone for Indian para-athletics — a first Commonwealth Games gold for a male para-athlete — and a 1-2 finish shows real depth in the discipline, not a one-off talent. It adds visibility and momentum to Indian para-sport heading toward future Paralympic cycles.
stories.ripple_effects: A high-profile Games-record gold typically brings sponsorship interest and government recognition (cash awards, jobs) that can help fund training for other rising para-athletes. It also raises the profile of grassroots talent-scouting in rural India, since Gavit was discovered doing farm work rather than through a formal sports academy.
stories.why_now: The win came on Day 6 of the ongoing Glasgow Commonwealth Games, as India's medal tally has been steadily climbing across athletics, boxing and weightlifting.
stories.watch_next: Watch India's remaining athletics events on July 30, including Neeraj Chopra's javelin qualifying and the shot put and discus finals.

key_terms.definition: A Paralympic/para-sport category for athletes competing with an impairment affecting one arm.

stories.the_lesson: Talent doesn't only come from formal academies — some of the best athletes are found in unlikely places, like a farm field, when someone is looking for it.

stories.title: Landslides shut 150+ roads in Himachal Pradesh, strand pilgrims on the Yamunotri highway in Uttarakhand
key_points: **152 roads** are shut across Himachal Pradesh after heavy rain triggered landslides and flash floods.
**57 of those closures are in Mandi district** alone; 68 water-supply schemes and 72 power transformers are also down.
Palampur recorded **133mm of rain in 24 hours**; IMD has issued an **orange alert** for four districts.
In Uttarakhand, landslides blocked **120 roads including three national highways**, stranding about **100 pilgrims** on the Yamunotri route for two days.
stories.background: Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand are Himalayan states whose narrow mountain roads are especially prone to landslides during India's **monsoon season** (roughly June to September), when saturated hillsides give way easily. Both states are also major pilgrimage corridors — Uttarakhand's **Char Dham** route, including Yamunotri, draws hundreds of thousands of pilgrims each monsoon despite the known risks, and road blockages there regularly strand travelers for days. This year's monsoon has already caused significant damage further east in **Assam**, so this is a second, separate flood/landslide emergency unfolding at the same time in the north.
stories.what_happened: As of **July 29**, **152 roads** are shut across Himachal Pradesh due to landslides and flash floods — the worst-hit district is **Mandi with 57 closures**, followed by Chamba (33), Kullu (31) and Shimla (14). The damage has also knocked out **68 water-supply schemes and 72 power transformers**. Palampur recorded **133mm of rain in just 24 hours**, prompting India's weather office to issue an **orange alert** (meaning be prepared, significant weather expected) for four districts through July 30. Next door in Uttarakhand, landslides have blocked **120 roads, including three national highways**, and around **100 pilgrims were stranded** on a washed-out stretch of the Yamunotri National Highway — part of the Char Dham pilgrimage route — for two days before being escorted across.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a second major Himalayan monsoon disaster running in parallel with the ongoing Assam floods, showing how widely this year's monsoon is straining India's infrastructure. Blocked national highways and downed power/water systems directly cut off supplies and strand travelers, including pilgrims who often have limited food or shelter options on these routes.
stories.ripple_effects: Local economies dependent on the Char Dham pilgrimage season — hotels, transport operators, food vendors — lose business every day the roads stay closed. Power and water outages compound the disruption for residents already isolated by blocked roads. Reconstruction costs for roads, transformers and water schemes will add to state disaster-relief budgets already stretched by Assam's floods.
stories.why_now: A burst of intense rainfall — Palampur's 133mm in 24 hours — triggered the latest wave of landslides, part of a broader pattern of unusually heavy monsoon rain hitting India's northern hill states this year.
stories.watch_next: Watch the IMD's orange alert through July 30 for whether rain intensifies further and whether more national highways in Uttarakhand get cut off.

key_terms.definition: India's second-highest weather warning level, meaning authorities should 'be prepared' for potentially disruptive, significant weather.
A famous four-shrine Hindu pilgrimage circuit in Uttarakhand's Himalayas, including Yamunotri, that draws huge crowds each year despite treacherous mountain roads.

stories.the_lesson: Mountain infrastructure is only as strong as its weakest link — a single washed-out stretch of highway can strand hundreds of people for days, even when the surrounding roads are fine, because there's often no alternate route through the Himalayas.

stories.title: India's Commonwealth Games medal count climbs into double digits, led by Mirabai Chanu's historic hat-trick gold
key_points: India's medal tally at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games has reached **12 medals** — 2 gold, 7 silver, 3 bronze — placing it **9th** on the table.
Weightlifter **Mirabai Chanu** delivered a **third consecutive Commonwealth Games gold**, breaking Games records in the snatch, clean & jerk and total (190kg) in the women's 48kg category.
Silvers have come from **Sarvesh Kushare** (high jump) and **Murali Sreeshankar** (long jump, his second CWG medal), plus three weightlifters.
**PM Modi** has been publicly congratulating each medalist as the tally builds.
Thursday brings more chances: **Neeraj Chopra** opens his javelin title defense and **Tajinderpal Singh Toor** goes into the shot put final.
stories.background: The 2026 Commonwealth Games are being held in **Glasgow, Scotland**, from July 23 to August 2 — the same city that hosted the 2014 Games, where a young Mirabai Chanu won her first CWG medal, a silver. She has won a medal at every Commonwealth Games since, culminating in Thursday's historic third straight gold. India has traditionally been strongest at these Games in weightlifting, wrestling, badminton and athletics, and this edition is following that pattern, with weightlifting supplying most of the country's medals in the opening week.
stories.what_happened: As of Thursday, India's medal tally at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games stood at **12** — 2 gold, 7 silver and 3 bronze — good for 9th place overall. The headline result came from weightlifter **Mirabai Chanu**, who won gold in the women's 48kg category with a total lift of **190kg** (an 85kg snatch and 105kg clean & jerk), breaking the Games record in all three categories and completing her third consecutive Commonwealth Games gold after Gold Coast 2018 and Birmingham 2022. Other medals have come from weightlifters Chanambam Rishikanta Singh, Raja Muthupandi and Valluri Ajaya Babu (silvers) and Bindyarani Devi Sorokhaibam (bronze), plus silvers from high jumper Sarvesh Kushare and long jumper **Murali Sreeshankar**, who became the first Indian man with two Commonwealth Games medals in that event. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has been publicly congratulating each medalist as results come in. India's campaign continues Thursday with javelin star **Neeraj Chopra** beginning his qualifying round, and shot putters Tajinderpal Singh Toor and Samardeep Singh Gill contesting the final, alongside weightlifting finals in the heavier categories.
stories.why_it_matters: The Commonwealth Games are one of India's most reliable sources of international medals, particularly in weightlifting and athletics, and strong performances here are often read as a barometer for the country's broader sporting depth heading into future Olympics.
stories.ripple_effects: Medal-winning performances typically translate into increased government sports funding attention and sponsorship interest for the athletes and their disciplines, particularly weightlifting given Chanu's sustained success. A strong javelin and shot put showing over the coming days would further boost India's athletics program, an area the country has invested heavily in since Neeraj Chopra's 2020 Olympic gold.
stories.why_now: The Games are roughly a week into their run (July 23–August 2), so the medal tally is a live, developing number that updates daily as more finals are contested.
stories.watch_next: Watch Thursday's javelin qualifying (Neeraj Chopra) and shot put final (Tajinderpal Singh Toor) for India's next potential medals.
stories.the_lesson: In multi-discipline events like the Commonwealth Games, a country's medal strength tends to concentrate in a handful of sports where it has built long-term coaching and funding pipelines — for India, that has consistently meant weightlifting and athletics.

stories.title: India and China's readout from the Beijing visit: both sides commit to peace on the disputed border

thread.previously: We reported that Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri concluded a two-day Beijing visit on July 29, meeting China's Vice Foreign Minister Hua Chunying and a Communist Party official, with both sides talking about framing each other as 'partners' rather than rivals — but without a concrete outcome beyond the tone of the talks.
thread.changed: The official Indian government readout now confirms a specific, substantive commitment: both sides reaffirmed the importance of maintaining peace and tranquility along the disputed Line of Actual Control (LAC), and Misri held an additional meeting with Li Wentang of the Communist Party's Central Party School — details not available when the visit merely 'wrapped up.'

key_points: India and China **reaffirmed maintaining peace along the LAC** (Line of Actual Control), the disputed Himalayan border.
The commitment came in the **official readout** from Foreign Secretary **Vikram Misri's** two-day Beijing visit.
Misri also met **Li Wentang**, Vice President of the Communist Party's **Central Party School**, to discuss future cooperation.
The talks build on efforts to implement an understanding reached between **PM Modi and President Xi Jinping**.
It follows Misri's earlier meetings with Vice Foreign Minister **Hua Chunying** and party official **Sun Haiyan**.
stories.background: India and China share a long, disputed Himalayan border called the **Line of Actual Control (LAC)** — there is no final, mutually agreed border line, which is why troop clashes (like the deadly 2020 Galwan Valley confrontation) have periodically flared. Since then, the two countries have been on a slow path toward normalizing ties: restoring some direct flights, easing visa rules, and resuming senior diplomatic visits, even as the underlying border dispute remains unresolved. **Vikram Misri**, India's Foreign Secretary, is the top career diplomat managing this delicate reset.
stories.what_happened: India's **Ministry of External Affairs (MEA)** released its official readout of Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri's two-day Beijing visit, confirming that both India and China **reaffirmed the importance of maintaining peace and tranquility along the LAC** — an explicit, mutual commitment on the border question that goes beyond the general 'partners not rivals' language reported when the visit first concluded. The MEA said Misri held **wide-ranging discussions** covering trade, cultural ties, people-to-people exchanges, and political engagement. Separate from his earlier meetings with Vice Foreign Minister **Hua Chunying** and Communist Party official **Sun Haiyan**, Misri also met **Li Wentang**, Vice President of the Communist Party's **Central Party School**, receiving a briefing on the institution's role and discussing future academic and policy exchanges between the two countries.
stories.why_it_matters: An explicit joint statement on preserving peace along a border where soldiers have died in clashes as recently as 2020 is a concrete, if modest, diplomatic marker — it signals both governments want to prevent the border dispute from derailing the broader normalization track, even though the underlying territorial disagreement remains unresolved.
stories.ripple_effects: A calmer border reduces the risk of a military miscalculation between two nuclear-armed neighbors and gives both governments more room to pursue economic engagement — potentially eased restrictions on Chinese investment, imports, or worker visas for Indian manufacturing projects that depend on Chinese equipment, an area closely watched by Indian electronics and solar companies.
stories.why_now: This is the formal government-to-government readout following Misri's visit, released after the visit's conclusion, and reflects both capitals wanting to lock in a specific, quotable commitment rather than leave the visit's outcome vague.
stories.watch_next: Whether this LAC commitment translates into any concrete de-escalation steps on the ground — troop pullbacks, resumed patrols, or a leader-level summit between Modi and Xi.

key_terms.definition: The de facto, disputed border between India and Chinese-controlled territory in the Himalayas — not a formally agreed international boundary, which is why both sides interpret it differently in places.

stories.the_lesson: In unresolved border disputes, diplomacy often can't solve the underlying disagreement — so it settles for the next best thing: an explicit, mutual commitment to keep the disagreement peaceful.
stories.market_link: Any follow-through on easing India's restrictions on Chinese investment or imports would matter for Indian electronics, solar, and auto-component manufacturers that depend on Chinese components.

stories.title: Supreme Court strikes down the rule letting projects get environmental clearance *after* they've already started
key_points: The Supreme Court **quashed a 2021 Office Memorandum** that let projects get **retrospective ('post-facto') environmental clearance**.
A **three-judge bench** led by **Chief Justice Surya Kant** ruled the Centre can't create such a bypass through a mere administrative order.
The Centre **can still allow post-facto clearances**, but only through a **valid statutory notification**, not an office memo.
Clearances already granted under the **2017 notification** and the now-**quashed 2021 memo** stay valid unless individually challenged.
The ruling applies **going forward only** — no new post-facto clearances can be issued under the scrapped mechanism.
stories.background: In India, most large projects — mines, factories, power plants, real estate — legally need an **environmental clearance (EC)** *before* construction begins, to assess and limit ecological damage upfront. Some companies have started projects without this approval and then sought clearance afterward, effectively asking regulators to forgive a fait accompli. In **2021**, the central government issued an **Office Memorandum (OM)** — a lower-level administrative order, not a law — creating a formal process for exactly that kind of after-the-fact approval, which environmental groups and courts have long argued undermines the entire point of the clearance system.
stories.what_happened: On **July 29**, a three-judge Supreme Court bench of **Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, and Justice Vipul Pancholi** unanimously **struck down the 2021 Office Memorandum** that had let the Centre grant environmental clearance to projects **after** they had already started construction or operations. The Court held that **prior environmental clearance is the cornerstone** of India's environmental regulatory framework and cannot be sidestepped through an executive order. It ruled the government **does** have the power to permit post-facto clearances, but only if it does so through a **valid statutory notification under Section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986** — not an internal memo. Clearances already granted under the 2017 notification or the now-scrapped 2021 memo will **continue to hold**, unless separately challenged in court, and the judgment applies **prospectively** — meaning no fresh clearances can be issued through the scrapped route from here on.
stories.why_it_matters: This closes a legal shortcut that let companies build first and seek environmental approval later — a workaround critics said let real damage happen before any regulatory check occurred. It's a reminder that the Supreme Court is willing to strike down convenient administrative fixes when they bypass the stricter process Parliament's own environmental law requires.
stories.ripple_effects: Companies and project developers who have historically relied on obtaining clearance after breaking ground now have a much narrower, more procedurally demanding path — future post-facto approvals must go through a formal, more visible statutory notification rather than a quiet office order, likely slowing that route and inviting more legal challenges to any existing clearances issued under the void memo.
stories.why_now: The ruling comes from a case that had been argued before the Court challenging the legality of the 2021 memo; the judgment was delivered this week as part of the Court's ongoing docket.
stories.watch_next: Whether the Centre issues a new statutory notification to formally re-establish a (narrower) post-facto clearance route, and whether any existing clearances granted under the voided 2021 memo face fresh individual legal challenges.

key_terms.definition: Environmental approval sought and granted *after* a project has already started construction or operations, rather than before — the reverse of how the process is meant to work.
An internal administrative order issued by a government department — a much lower legal bar than a law passed by Parliament or a formal statutory notification.

stories.the_lesson: A regulatory rule is only as strong as the process used to create it — courts will often let a government reach the same practical outcome, but insist it be done through the harder, more accountable legal route rather than a quiet shortcut.
stories.market_link: Raises compliance uncertainty for infrastructure, mining, and industrial companies that have relied on after-the-fact clearances, and could slow project timelines in sectors like cement, power, and real estate.

stories.title: India's goods exports rise 15% in early FY27, and the first tranche of the India-US trade deal is 'ready' once tariffs are settled, says Goyal
key_points: India's merchandise exports grew roughly **15%** in FY27 so far (April-July)
That puts exports on track past **$170 billion** for the period
The first tranche of the **India-US trade deal** is negotiated and ready to activate
The deal is stuck on India getting a **tariff edge** over rival exporters like those in ASEAN
India still targets **$1 trillion** in total exports for FY27
stories.background: India and the US have spent much of 2026 negotiating a Bilateral Trade Agreement, first announced by Modi and Trump in February. Talks got complicated after the US Supreme Court struck down the tariff mechanism (called IEEPA) Washington had been using, forcing a shift to a different legal tariff structure, and after the US separately raised tariffs on India tied to its continued purchases of Russian oil. Exporters have been waiting in limbo for the tariff picture to clear up.
stories.what_happened: Commerce and Industry Minister **Piyush Goyal** said on **Wednesday, July 29**, that India's merchandise exports have grown about **15%** so far in FY27 (April-July) versus roughly $148.58 billion in the same period last year — putting the period on track to cross **$170 billion**, despite the Red Sea shipping crisis and broader global trade turbulence. He also said the first tranche of the proposed India-US trade deal is fully negotiated and ready to be activated, but is waiting on the US to grant India a competitive tariff edge over rival exporters such as those in ASEAN countries. Goyal reiterated India's FY27 target of **$1 trillion in total exports** ($530bn in goods plus $470bn in services), crediting new free-trade deals with the UK and Oman for supporting the momentum.
stories.why_it_matters: The 15% export growth is a concrete positive data point that pushes back against the gloomier picture of a weak monsoon and trade shocks weighing on India's economy this year, and Goyal's comments spell out exactly what's still blocking the India-US trade deal from taking effect.
stories.ripple_effects: Strong export data could support the rupee and sentiment in export-heavy sectors like IT, pharma and textiles — sectors already rallying on the Sensex today — while continued uncertainty on the tariff structure keeps exporters cautious about pricing new US contracts.
stories.why_now: Goyal's comments came alongside the release of fresh year-to-date trade data at a New Delhi event on Wednesday.
stories.watch_next: Whether the US actually issues the order cutting India's tariff (reportedly targeted around 18%), and whether the two sides formally sign the trade deal's first tranche.

key_terms.definition: Tariffs the US had imposed using an emergency-powers law, later struck down by the US Supreme Court, forcing Washington to use a different legal basis for tariffs.

stories.the_lesson: Trade deals rarely fail over big-picture disagreement — they often stall on one narrow technical sticking point, like a comparative tariff rate, that has to be resolved before everything else can move.
stories.market_link: The Indian rupee, IT/pharma/textile exporters, Reliance Industries and Indian Oil Corp (Russian-crude exposure), Sensex/Nifty.

stories.title: Murali Sreeshankar wins long jump silver at the Commonwealth Games, becomes the first Indian man with two CWG medals in the event
key_points: Sreeshankar leapt **8.09m** for silver, just **1cm** behind bronze
Jamaica's **Tajay Gayle** won gold with **8.15m**
It's India's **13th medal** of the Glasgow Games
First Indian man ever with **two CWG long-jump medals** (also silver at Birmingham 2022)
stories.background: Murali Sreeshankar is an Olympian and one of India's most decorated long jumpers, and long jump has been one of India's stronger events at the Commonwealth Games. He won silver at the last Games in Birmingham in 2022 and has been chasing a first CWG gold ever since. This is a separate discipline — athletics — from the boxing medals India has already won at these Games.
stories.what_happened: In the men's long jump final at the Commonwealth Games 2026 in Glasgow, **Murali Sreeshankar won silver** with a best jump of **8.09 metres**. Jamaica's Tajay Gayle took gold with 8.15m, while Scotland's Stephen Mackenzie won bronze at 8.08m — just a centimetre behind Sreeshankar in a razor-tight final. The medal is **India's 13th of the Games** and makes Sreeshankar the first Indian man to win two Commonwealth Games long-jump medals, adding to his Birmingham 2022 silver.
stories.why_it_matters: It's a historic individual milestone for Indian athletics and keeps India's strong medal momentum going at these Games, alongside its boxing squad's run.
stories.ripple_effects: Adds to India's overall medal tally and athletics narrative at CWG 2026, and raises Sreeshankar's profile heading into the next Asian Games and Olympic cycle.
stories.why_now: The final was held on Day 6 of the Glasgow Games, competition day July 29.
stories.watch_next: India's remaining athletics and boxing finals in the closing days of CWG 2026, and the country's final medal tally versus Birmingham 2022.
stories.the_lesson: Consistency across multiple Games — not just a single great performance — is what turns an athlete into a record-holder; Sreeshankar's second medal in the same event, four years apart, is the harder achievement.

stories.title: Rajya Sabha passes bill making it a crime to insult India's national song, Vande Mataram
key_points: The **Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026** passed by voice vote in the Rajya Sabha
It extends the same legal protection already given to the **national flag, Constitution, and national anthem** to the national song, Vande Mataram
Deliberately insulting it or obstructing its singing can now bring up to **three years in prison**
The Opposition, led by Congress, **walked out** in protest during the debate
It amends the **Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971**
stories.background: **Vande Mataram** ('I Bow to Thee, Mother') is India's national song, distinct from the national anthem (Jana Gana Mana), written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay and closely tied to India's independence movement. Since 1971, a law has made it a criminal offence to insult the **national flag**, the **Constitution**, or the **national anthem** — but the national song had never carried the same legal protection. The debate over extending that protection has periodically resurfaced, including around Vande Mataram's 150th anniversary events in late 2025.
stories.what_happened: On Wednesday, the **Rajya Sabha** (the upper house of India's Parliament) passed the **Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026** by voice vote, extending the 1971 Act's protections to Vande Mataram for the first time. Under the amended law, anyone who **intentionally prevents or obstructs** the singing of the national song, or who commits a **deliberate act of insult or disrespect** toward it, can face up to **three years in prison** or a fine. The bill was taken up for debate in the post-lunch session, and Opposition MPs — including members of the Congress party and the CPI(M) — objected during the discussion and **walked out** of the House in protest before the vote.
stories.why_it_matters: This gives Vande Mataram the same criminal-law status as the flag and national anthem, meaning disputes over how or whether it's sung — in schools, public events, or protests — now carry potential legal consequences rather than just being a matter of custom or etiquette.
stories.ripple_effects: The law could affect institutions like schools and local government bodies, where singing (or refusing to sing) the national song has occasionally been politically contentious. It also lands amid a broader pattern of legislation this session — like the anti-paper-leak bill — that has drawn similarly sharp Opposition pushback.
stories.why_now: The bill was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on July 24, 2026, and passed five days later as part of the ongoing Monsoon Session of Parliament.
stories.watch_next: Whether the Lok Sabha (the lower house) takes up and passes the same bill to make it law, and how it is implemented in schools and public institutions.

key_terms.definition: The upper house of India's Parliament, whose members are elected indirectly by state legislatures rather than directly by voters.

stories.the_lesson: Symbols carry different legal weight depending on what law protects them — the same national song can go from a matter of tradition to a matter of criminal law with a single act of Parliament.

stories.title: Shane McDermott quits Pakistan's coaching staff to become Afghanistan's fielding coach
key_points: The **Afghanistan Cricket Board (ACB)** confirmed Shane McDermott as its new **assistant and fielding coach** on July 29, 2026.
McDermott **resigned from the Pakistan Cricket Board** on July 18, after a year in the same fielding-coach role there.
He previously worked with **Afghanistan from January 2024 to July 2025**, before his stint with Pakistan.
He is set to **join the Afghanistan squad on August 1**, ahead of a **five-match ODI series against Ireland**.
The move is a rare case of a coach switching directly **between two rival national teams** within the same year.
stories.background: International cricket coaching staff — batting, bowling, and fielding coaches — frequently move between national teams, but doing so between two sides that regularly play each other, like Afghanistan and Pakistan, is unusual and can draw scrutiny over potential conflicts of interest, since the coach knows a rival team's methods and personnel intimately. Fielding coaches specifically work on catching, ground fielding, and athleticism — an area increasingly seen as a difference-maker in modern limited-overs cricket.
stories.what_happened: The **Afghanistan Cricket Board officially confirmed** on July 29, 2026 that Shane McDermott has been appointed the national team's new **Assistant and Fielding Coach**. McDermott previously held the same fielding-coach role with Afghanistan from **January 2024 to July 2025**, before moving to a similar position with the **Pakistan Cricket Board from July 2025**. He resigned from the Pakistan role on **July 18, 2026**, roughly eighteen days before his new Afghanistan appointment was confirmed. McDermott is scheduled to formally **join Afghanistan's coaching staff on August 1, 2026**, in time to prepare the team for its upcoming **five-match ODI series against Ireland**.
stories.why_it_matters: Fielding standards have become a genuine competitive differentiator in modern white-ball cricket, and a coach who knows Pakistan's methods intimately now works for one of its regional rivals — a small but real edge for Afghanistan, and a talking point about coaching-market movement between competing cricket boards.
stories.ripple_effects: Afghanistan gets an experienced fielding coach with recent, direct knowledge of a key rival team just as it heads into a big ODI series — potentially sharpening Afghanistan's fielding standards quickly, given McDermott already has a working relationship with several of the squad's senior players from his earlier stint.
stories.why_now: The appointment is surfacing today because the ACB's confirmation came July 29, 2026, with McDermott's formal start date just days away on August 1.
stories.watch_next: Watch Afghanistan's fielding performance in the opening ODI of the Ireland series for an early read on McDermott's impact.
stories.the_lesson: Specialist expertise — like fielding coaching — increasingly moves across boundaries and rivalries in professional sport, because the value of the skill outweighs old loyalties.

stories.title: England captain Nat Sciver-Brunt targets a return to bowling — but may sit out the Ireland ODIs
key_points: Sciver-Brunt says she **doesn't want to give up bowling** despite a recurring calf injury, targeting an all-rounder comeback.
She suffered the injury during **The Hundred**, England's domestic short-format tournament, earlier this month.
She has **hinted she may miss** England's ODI series against Ireland next month to protect her recovery.
Her rehab is being **carefully managed** by England's medical and performance staff to avoid a repeat injury.
As **England Women's captain**, her fitness directly affects the team's balance ahead of a busy international calendar.
stories.background: **Nat Sciver-Brunt** is England Women's captain and one of the team's most important all-rounders, meaning she contributes as both a top-order batter and a bowler, giving England extra tactical flexibility. Losing her bowling contribution, even temporarily, forces England to rebalance its bowling attack and batting order. She picked up a calf injury — a strain in the lower leg muscle — while playing in **The Hundred**, England's short, fast domestic cricket competition that runs through the English summer.
stories.what_happened: Nat Sciver-Brunt said in comments published July 30, 2026 that she is determined to return to bowling as soon as her recovery allows, stating 'I don't want to give up the bowling just yet,' after sustaining a **calf injury** during The Hundred earlier this month. She confirmed she is currently focused on rehabilitation and that her return is being carefully staged by England's medical and performance staff specifically to avoid the injury recurring. Sciver-Brunt has **hinted she could miss England's ODI series against Ireland next month** in order to prioritise a full recovery over rushing back for a lower-stakes series, with her sights instead set on being fully fit for bigger assignments later in the international calendar.
stories.why_it_matters: As captain and a genuine all-rounder, Sciver-Brunt's fitness is a significant factor in England Women's team balance — her absence changes both the batting order and bowling options, and any recurring calf issue raises longer-term fitness-management questions ahead of the team's biggest upcoming series.
stories.ripple_effects: If she does sit out the Ireland series, England will need to test alternative bowling and batting-order combinations without their captain, giving other players a chance to step up and giving team management valuable data on squad depth ahead of bigger tournaments.
stories.why_now: Her comments came today, July 30, 2026, as she updates fans and media on her recovery timeline ahead of squad selection for the Ireland series.
stories.watch_next: Watch for England's official squad announcement for the Ireland ODI series to see whether Sciver-Brunt is included.

key_terms.definition: A cricket player skilled at both batting and bowling, giving their team extra flexibility in team selection and tactics.

stories.the_lesson: In sport, protecting a slow, proper recovery from a recurring injury is often the higher-value long-term decision, even when it means missing a nearer-term match.

stories.title: Stephen Fleming set to become England's new Test coach, replacing Brendon McCullum
key_points: Former **New Zealand captain Stephen Fleming** has emerged as the clear frontrunner to become England's new **Test head coach**.
The **ECB (England and Wales Cricket Board)** is reportedly close to confirming Fleming's appointment after a round of interviews concluded this week.
Fleming, 53, would replace fellow Kiwi **Brendon McCullum**, who is leaving the Test role.

He beat out competition including English coaches **Richard Dawson and Jonathan Trott**, and Australian **Tom Moody**; early favorite **Andy Flower** withdrew to focus on his franchise coaching roles.

The ECB is expected to let assistant coach **Marcus Trescothick** lead the team on an **interim basis** for the upcoming Pakistan series, with Fleming taking full charge for the **December tour of South Africa**.
stories.background: Brendon McCullum has coached England's Test team since 2022, helping popularize the aggressive 'Bazball' approach to Test cricket that transformed the team's results and style of play. Stephen Fleming, one of New Zealand's most respected former captains with **111 Test caps**, has built a second career as a hugely successful franchise coach — he has won **five IPL titles with Chennai Super Kings** and has also coached CSK's sister franchises in South Africa's SA20 and the US's Major League Cricket. He also has roots in English cricket, having played for Middlesex, Yorkshire and Nottinghamshire and coached Southern Brave in England's Hundred competition.
stories.what_happened: **Stephen Fleming has emerged as the favourite to become England's new Test head coach**, with the ECB reportedly close to finalizing his appointment after interviews wrapped up this week. He is set to **replace Brendon McCullum**, who is stepping away from the Test coaching role. Fleming saw off competition from English coaches Richard Dawson and Jonathan Trott and Australia's Tom Moody, while earlier favourite **Andy Flower withdrew** from consideration to concentrate on his existing franchise commitments with Royal Challengers Bengaluru and London Spirit. Because Fleming has ongoing IPL and franchise obligations, the ECB is expected to have **assistant coach Marcus Trescothick take interim charge** of the team for the upcoming **Test series against Pakistan**, with Fleming stepping in to lead the side fully for **December's tour of South Africa**.
stories.why_it_matters: England's Test coaching job is one of the most scrutinized roles in world cricket, and this appointment marks the end of the high-profile, high-scoring 'Bazball' era under McCullum. Fleming's franchise-honed coaching style and calm reputation would mark a real change in tone for a team known lately for aggression and risk-taking.
stories.ripple_effects: Fleming's move creates a coaching vacancy question at Chennai Super Kings and his other franchise sides, and gives England's players an interim adjustment period under Trescothick before their new permanent coach fully arrives. It could also reshape England's tactical approach heading into major series against Pakistan and South Africa.
stories.why_now: The ECB's coaching search concluded its interview round this week, with reports of Fleming's frontrunner status and the interim Trescothick plan surfacing together as the decision neared.
stories.watch_next: Official confirmation of Fleming's appointment by the ECB, and how Trescothick's England side performs in the interim Pakistan Test series starting August 19 at Headingley.
stories.the_lesson: In cricket coaching, franchise success increasingly counts as much as international playing pedigree when national boards choose a head coach — it's now a genuinely global coaching marketplace.

stories.title: Retired legends of Indian, Pakistani, Sri Lankan and Afghan cricket kick off Season 2 of the Asian Legends League in Zambia
key_points: The **Asian Legends League Season 2** launches today in **Lusaka, Zambia**, running through **August 10**.
The opener pits the **Sri Lankan Lions against the Afghanistan Pathans**, captained by **Thisara Perera** and **Asghar Afghan**.
Six teams of **retired international stars** compete across **19 matches** over less than two weeks.
Marquee names include **Yusuf Pathan** (Indian Royals), **Shakib Al Hasan** (Bangladesh Tigers), and **Mohammad Hafeez** (Pakistan Panthers).
The tournament is part of a growing wave of **legends' T20 leagues** that let recently retired stars keep playing competitively — and keep fans watching them.
stories.background: 'Legends leagues' are a relatively new format in cricket: short T20 tournaments built entirely around **recently retired international players**, letting fans watch familiar stars in competitive cricket again without the demands of the international calendar. They've grown popular across South Asia because the region's cricket fandom is intensely personality-driven, and many retired stars remain marketable well past their playing days. The Asian Legends League specifically brings together former internationals from **India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan** — a rare format where players from countries that rarely tour each other bilaterally (India and Pakistan chief among them) share a tournament.
stories.what_happened: Season 2 of the **Asian Legends League** begins today, July 30, in **Lusaka, Zambia**, opening with a **jersey unveiling ceremony** ahead of the tournament's first match between the **Sri Lankan Lions**, captained by **Thisara Perera**, and the **Afghanistan Pathans**, led by **Asghar Afghan**. The competition runs for less than two weeks, wrapping up with a **grand final on August 10**, and features **six teams playing 19 matches** in total. The other four teams are the **Indian Royals** (led by Yusuf Pathan), the **Bangladesh Tigers** (led by Shakib Al Hasan), the **Pakistan Panthers** (led by Mohammad Hafeez), and a composite **Rest of Asian Stars** side (led by Tillakaratne Dilshan). A double-header follows on July 31 with the Pakistan Panthers facing the Rest of Asian Stars, and the Indian Royals playing the Bangladesh Tigers.
stories.why_it_matters: Beyond the nostalgia factor, these leagues have become a real secondary revenue stream and fan-engagement vehicle for cricket boards and retired players alike, and this edition is notable for assembling players from countries — India and Pakistan especially — that rarely share a cricket pitch in bilateral series anymore.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect broadcast and sponsorship interest from South Asian markets given the star power involved, and continued growth of the 'legends league' model globally if this season draws strong viewership, similar to how the Road Safety World Series and Legends League Cricket have grown in recent years.
stories.why_now: The tournament's second season was scheduled for this window on the global cricket calendar, launching today with its opening ceremony and first match.
stories.watch_next: How the Indian Royals vs Bangladesh Tigers double-header opener on July 31 performs in viewership, and the group standings heading into the August 10 final.
stories.the_lesson: Cricket's economics increasingly extend well past a player's international career — retired stars remain valuable draws, and leagues built purely around nostalgia and star power can thrive alongside the traditional international game.

stories.title: Zaheer Abbas backs Kohli and Rohit for the 2027 World Cup, but tells Rohit to sharpen his fitness
key_points: Former Pakistan captain **Zaheer Abbas** says age 'should not be a factor' for Kohli and Rohit at the **2027 ODI World Cup**
He said **Kohli is 'still supremely fit'**, while **Rohit needs to pay more attention to fitness**
Comes after both scored heavily in India's recent **ODI series against England**, including Rohit's maiden Lord's ODI century
The pair next play together in a home ODI series against the **West Indies starting in September**
It contrasts with earlier comments from **Sourav Ganguly**, who said neither is a certainty for 2027
stories.background: Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli, two of India's most decorated batters, have faced persistent questions about their long-term futures in ODI cricket as they approach their late 30s, with selectors and former players publicly split on whether they should be automatic picks for the 2027 ODI World Cup, to be co-hosted in Africa. Former India captain Sourav Ganguly recently said publicly that neither man's spot should be considered guaranteed.
stories.what_happened: Pakistan batting great **Zaheer Abbas** has publicly backed both **Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli** to play the 2027 ODI World Cup, saying **'age should not be a factor as long as they are fit and continue scoring runs.'** On fitness specifically, he said **'Kohli is still supremely fit, while Rohit just needs to pay a little more attention to his fitness.'** The comments follow a strong recent ODI series for India in England, where **Rohit scored his maiden ODI century at Lord's** in the series-deciding final match and **Kohli struck twin fifties**. Both players are next set to feature together in a **home ODI series against the West Indies starting in September**.
stories.why_it_matters: With India's selectors reportedly weighing a generational transition in ODI cricket, high-profile endorsements like this one from a respected rival great add public pressure to the debate over whether experience or age should decide World Cup selection.
stories.ripple_effects: Continued strong form plus vocal support from figures like Zaheer Abbas makes it harder for selectors to drop either player without public backlash, while any dip in fitness or form before 2027 would immediately reignite the opposite argument.
stories.why_now: The comments follow directly from India's just-finished ODI series in England, where both players' performances gave immediate, fresh evidence for the debate over their World Cup futures.
stories.watch_next: How Rohit and Kohli perform in September's home ODI series against the West Indies, the next major form checkpoint before 2027 squad conversations intensify.
stories.the_lesson: In selection debates, a good current run of form buys senior players time — but it doesn't settle the underlying question of long-term transition, which resurfaces the moment form dips.

stories.title: CSK re-emerges as front-runner for Hardik Pandya as IPL's biggest trade saga drags on
key_points: Reports now say **Chennai Super Kings is 'emerging as the leading candidate'** to sign Hardik Pandya
CSK is offering a **cash-plus-one-player** package built around **Shivam Dube**
Mumbai Indians still want **Shivam Dube and Ayush Mhatre**; CSK continues to **refuse to include Mhatre**
**Delhi Capitals'** rival offer of Axar Patel and Prithvi Shaw appears to have lost momentum
None of the trade talk has been **officially confirmed** by any of the three franchises involved
stories.background: Mumbai Indians and Chennai Super Kings have been in advanced, unconfirmed talks for weeks over trading MI captain Hardik Pandya to CSK. MI's original ask was Shivam Dube and rising batter Ayush Mhatre; CSK refused to part with Mhatre and countered with Dube, South African batter Dewald Brevis, and roughly ₹10 crore in cash. When that stalled, Delhi Capitals entered the picture offering captain Axar Patel and opener Prithvi Shaw, with Kolkata Knight Riders floated as a fallback if the MI-CSK deal collapsed entirely.
stories.what_happened: The trade saga has swung back toward Chennai: multiple reports now describe **CSK as the leading candidate** to land Pandya, offering a deal centred on **Shivam Dube plus additional cash**, rather than including Ayush Mhatre as MI originally wanted. Mumbai's demand for Mhatre alongside Dube remains a sticking point, and CSK is holding firm in refusing to include the young batter. The rival bid from **Delhi Capitals** (Axar Patel and Prithvi Shaw) — which had appeared to gain ground in recent days — seems to have lost momentum as CSK re-asserts itself as the front-runner. As with every stage of this saga, **no franchise has made an official statement**, and all reporting remains speculative.
stories.why_it_matters: If completed, this would be one of the largest trades in IPL history, reshaping the leadership and balance of two of the league's biggest franchises ahead of the 2027 mini-auction — and the back-and-forth shows how fluid even 'advanced' trade talks can be.
stories.ripple_effects: A Pandya-to-CSK move would leave Mumbai Indians needing a new captain and all-rounder, reshuffle Chennai's middle order, and could push Delhi Capitals and Kolkata Knight Riders toward other trade or auction targets instead.
stories.why_now: This is surfacing today because the IPL's trade window is active ahead of the 2027 mini-auction, and each new counter-offer between the franchises is being reported as it leaks out.
stories.watch_next: Whether either MI or CSK moves off its current position on including Ayush Mhatre, which has been the central sticking point throughout.

key_terms.definition: A smaller IPL auction held between full mega-auctions, used by franchises to fill a limited number of squad gaps — trades are often finalised just before it.

stories.the_lesson: In trade negotiations, the 'leading candidate' can flip within days when no deal is actually signed — treat unconfirmed reports as a snapshot of leverage, not a done deal.

thread.previously: We reported Delhi Capitals had entered the Pandya trade race with an Axar Patel-Prithvi Shaw offer after MI and CSK stalled over CSK's refusal to include Ayush Mhatre, with Kolkata Knight Riders floated as a fallback.
thread.changed: Momentum has swung back to Chennai, with CSK now reported as the leading candidate on a cash-plus-Dube package, while Delhi's rival offer appears to have cooled.
